adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The old grain warehouse on the east bank of the river had stood empty for eleven years before the city council finally agreed to convert it into a public library and community centre. The bidding process took most of 2018, and the contract was awarded to a consortium of local firms who promised to keep as much of the original timber frame as possible. Work began the following March, when the first surveyors arrived to measure the brick walls and record every crack and stain left by decades of grain dust.

The early months were dominated by structural questions. Engineers found that two of the roof trusses had rotted through where rainwater had seeped in behind the gutters, and the north wall had begun to lean outward by almost a foot. Bracing the wall required a temporary steel frame, which had to be threaded through gaps cut in the brickwork and anchored into the foundations. Neighbours complained about the noise for most of the summer, and the council held three public meetings to explain why the work could not be delayed.

By the autumn the shell of the building was secure and the interior could be divided into rooms. The architect in charge, a quiet woman who had spent a decade restoring churches in the north, insisted on keeping the brick visible wherever possible rather than covering it with plasterboard. Her drawings showed a children's reading room in the old weighbridge house, a small auditorium under the western eaves, and a cafe along the southern wall where the loading doors had once opened onto the wharf.

Money was the constant difficulty. The original budget had been set before the roof survey, and every additional repair pushed the total higher. A grant from a national heritage fund covered part of the shortfall, but the remainder had to be raised locally, and the fund-raising committee spent two years organising concerts, raffles and sponsored walks. The project director, who had previously managed a hospital extension in the same city, was credited afterwards with keeping the whole thing on schedule despite the constant revisions.

Public consultation shaped the smaller decisions. Residents of the streets immediately behind the warehouse asked for a garden instead of a car park, and they got one, though it was smaller than they had hoped and sloped awkwardly toward the river. Older residents asked for a room where clubs could meet during the day, and this became a modest space on the ground floor with a kitchenette and a long table. Younger families wanted somewhere to leave pushchairs and bicycles, which led to a covered rack beside the main entrance.

The opening ceremony was held on a cold Saturday in February, with the mayor cutting a ribbon while a school choir sang slightly out of tune. Inside, the shelves were still half empty, and the smell of fresh paint hung over everything. The head librarian had been hired only six weeks earlier and had barely finished interviewing staff; her assistant arrived on the first morning carrying a box of cataloguing manuals, and the two of them spent the whole day labelling the fiction section.

Six years on, the building has settled into its role. The garden is overgrown in places and the cafe has changed hands twice, but the reading room is busy every afternoon and the auditorium hosts film nights, lectures and the occasional wedding reception. The council occasionally discusses a second conversion on the west bank, though nothing has been agreed, and the cost of the first project is still cited in every debate about whether such restorations are worth the money.
